paras: The Akron riot of 1900 was a night of mob violence in Akron, Ohio, on August 22, 1900, when a crowd of thousands tried to seize and lynch Louis Peck, a Black prisoner accused of attempting to assault a six-year-old white girl. Peck had been moved to Cleveland, and the crowd fought the police, looted a hardware store, and burned and dynamited the city building. Two children were killed and about twenty people wounded, and Peck was sentenced to life two days later in a hearing that lasted minutes.

According to the wire, Peck offered Christina Maas a buggy ride on Monday night, August 20, and she was found hours later by a road west of the city. Arrested early on August 22, he reportedly confessed to Prisonkeeper John E. Washer and was bound over, and as word spread officers learned that an attempt would be made to lynch him. At 4 p.m. Sheriff Kelly took him and another Black prisoner, Bud Howard, to the Cleveland jail.

That evening a crowd gathered at the city prison "yelling for the life of Peck," including about 500 men from Perkins hill headed by the girl's father. It forced its way into the prison, the county jail, where a committee was allowed to search the cells, and the court house, and would not believe Mayor W. E. Young that Peck was gone; a Black man passing by was kicked and cuffed.

After 10 p.m. shots were exchanged with the police in the city building, and the crowd then looted guns from the Standard Hardware store and set Columbia hall afire. At 1:45 a.m., after the officers had released the prisoners and fled, dynamite wrecked the city building, which then burned. Glen Wade, 10 or 11, was shot through the heart, and four-year-old Rhoda Davidson was shot in her mother's arms and died on August 24. Militia companies arrived on the morning of August 23.

Saloons were closed and martial law kept through August 26. Authorities named about 30 rioters, and by September 5 a special grand jury was hearing witnesses and one man, Harvey Earl, had pleaded guilty to rioting. No indictment of rioters or inquest appears in the coverage.

On August 24 Peck, who had begged Washer to shoot him if a mob waited, was brought back under guard, indicted for rape, and sentenced to life by Judge D. J. Nye on his guilty plea, all in about five minutes.

White papers carried the story on August 23 under headlines such as "SIX KILLED IN AN OHIO RIOT" and "RAPIST PECK LOCKED UP," treating Peck's guilt as settled. The Akron Daily Democrat called it "A NIGHT OF TERROR" but judged the five-minute sentence "quickly, but not too soon." Southern papers used it against Northern critics: the Richmond Times said Northern whites would act as Southern whites had, and the Sherman Register, quoted in the Houston Post, said Peck should have been sentenced to death.

Black weeklies reprinted the wire, but their editorials condemned the mob: the Afro-American Advance saw "an epidemic of Negrophobia" moving north, and the Richmond Planet protested a double standard in punishment and ended "Lynch-law must go!" The Cleveland Gazette alone questioned the conviction, arguing that Peck had pleaded guilty "by threats of being taken back to the mob" and contrasting his life term with four years given a white man on a like charge.

The first dispatch reported six dead, but later lists and Rhoda Davidson's death support two. The Akron Daily Democrat's headline blamed police volleys for the killing, while Chief Harrison said his men fired into the air and the deaths came from "chance shots."

reader.title: Akron riot of 1900
bases: A crowd of thousands tried to take Louis Peck, a Black prisoner accused of attempting to assault a white child, from the Akron city prison and county jail in order to kill him; finding him gone, it fought the police, looted a store, and burned and dynamited the city building (A2, A3, A5, A9).

The mob sought Peck to lynch him over a crime accusation but never reached him, since he had been moved to Cleveland and was later sentenced by a court (A2, A26); the two people who died were children in or near the crowd, shot during the exchange of fire between mob and police, not victims of the mob's lynching aim (A2, A9, A32).

The local Akron Daily Democrat, several independently worded wire versions, and Black weeklies agree on the jail searches, the removal of Peck, the fighting, fires and dynamite, and the two deaths (A2, A3, A5, A9, A26).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A crowd of thousands searched the prison, jail and court house for Peck, refused to believe he had been moved, attacked the city building, exchanged fire with police, looted guns, and burned and dynamited the building; two children died.

accounts.label: Akron Daily Democrat (local)
accounts.gist: Its headline said police volleys into the crowd killed one and wounded citizens, which 'inflamed the crowd' into further bloodshed and destruction.

accounts.label: Chief of police
accounts.gist: Harrison said police fired into the air without his orders, a man in the crowd then fired into the building, he ordered firing stopped, and the deaths came from 'chance shots'.

accounts.label: Peck's statements
accounts.gist: In Cleveland Peck said he was arrested Tuesday and removed about 2 p.m. Wednesday; he admitted a crime while drunk but said he would plead guilty only if the penalty were not life.

accounts.label: Cleveland Gazette (Black editorial)
accounts.gist: Peck was forced to plead guilty by threats of being returned to the mob and was guilty only of assault; his life term contrasted with a white man's four years for a like charge.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'RAPIST PECK LOCKED UP. His Life Sought By a Frenzied Akron Mob' and 'SIX KILLED IN AN OHIO RIOT' treated Peck's guilt as settled and the riot as a calamity.
The Akron Daily Democrat headlined 'AKRON HAD A NIGHT OF TERROR!' and called the destruction malicious, while welcoming the five-minute sentence as 'not too soon'.
Southern papers used Akron against Northern critics of lynching; the Sherman Register wished Peck had been sentenced to death, while the Columbia Herald said mobs should be 'shot down'.
The Wisconsin Weekly Advocate, Iowa Bystander and Afro-American Advance ran wire copy, including the headline phrase 'Intent on Lynching Negro Rapist'.
Black editorials called the riot 'Negrophobia' spreading north, demanded the mob's arrest, and attacked a double standard in punishment ('Lynch-law must go!').
The Cleveland Gazette questioned Peck's forced plea and life sentence and urged prosecution of the mob's leaders.

info: Riot on the night of Wednesday, Aug. 22, 1900, from about 7:30 p.m. until near dawn on Aug. 23; the alleged assault was on Monday night, Aug. 20.
Downtown Akron: the city prison and city building, the county jail and court house, the Standard Hardware Company store on Main Street, and Columbia hall next to the city building.

Target: Louis (also 'Lewis', 'Pock') Peck, described as a negro, 30, 35 or 36 years old, married with one child; he was not reached. Dead: Glen (Glenn, Clem) Wade, 10 or 11, and Rhoda Davidson, 4. About 16 to 20 others wounded, among them Fred Vorwerk, firemen and policemen. An unnamed Black passerby was kicked and cuffed.

Peck was accused of attempting to assault Christina (Tina) Maas, 6 (four in one report), daughter of Theodore Maas, after offering her a buggy ride on Monday night; he was reported to have confessed to the prisonkeeper and to a Cleveland deputy, and was indicted for rape.

An unnamed crowd, described as 'chiefly of workingmen', including about 500 from Perkins hill headed by the girl's father; the Seattle Republican called it 'ignorant foreigners and city slums'. Later arrests named Harvey Earl and Edward Eppley; Frank Sickles was charged with shooting.
No Black person was reported killed.
Peck was sentenced to life imprisonment and taken to the Columbus penitentiary the same night; the first 30 days were to be in solitary confinement.
